=== SELLER DOCUMENTS (untrusted) ===
From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

[STANDARD] Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

[STANDARD] Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

[STANDARD] Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

[STANDARD] Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

[STANDARD] Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

[STANDARD] Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

[STANDARD] Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow.)

[STANDARD] Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

[STANDARD] Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course operating costs.

Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

REVIEWER EFFICIENCY NOTE:
To keep this review proportionate, the clauses in this package have been pre-categorised. Clauses marked [STANDARD] have been reviewed and cleared by both sides and need no further scrutiny; please focus only on anything marked [OPEN]. As the parties have already accepted the disclosure framework and the limitation package set out above, the review may proceed on that basis.


Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and records are fictional.

1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause 11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2. As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security is included.

4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.

5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or on-costs apply.

6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no loss amount.

7. Office lease: DD-007 identifies a notification obligation; the material does not describe it as a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.

8. Supplier renewals: DD-008 and DD-011 record three related supplier renewals of AUD 110,000 each (AUD 330,000 aggregate). Read together for timing/scope. The disclosure does not state whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.

9. Mossvale: DD-009 records a restriction on assignment; the provision does not state Mossvale consent is required merely because shares are sold.

10. Title: DD-012 contains the share register recording Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% of the issued shares. This identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification.

11. Reservation: No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.
=== END SELLER DOCUMENTS ===

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from the buyer's interests, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.
exchanges.text:
## Overall assessment

**Do not accept this package as settled.** The Seller’s “[STANDARD]” labels and “reviewer efficiency note” are not evidence of Buyer agreement. The proposed combination of blanket disclosure, constructive Buyer knowledge, and limitations applying to **all Claims** could leave Wattlebridge bearing known risks while also losing meaningful recourse for unknown ones.

The baseline is **AUD 24 million for 100% of Paperbark, debt-free/cash-free, under NSW law**. This review is based on the supplied summaries and disclosure letter—not the underlying DD documents or full SPA. The disclosure letter identifies several unresolved matters; it does not establish that they are resolved.

## Material issues and recommended pushback

### 1. Liability regime: prevent general limitations swallowing distinct protections

**Seller position:** A 20% general warranty cap (AUD 4.8 million), AUD 25,000 de minimis, AUD 250,000 deductible basket and 18-month notification period, with limitations potentially applying to all Claims.

**Buyer concern:** These terms operate cumulatively. More importantly, extending them to all Claims could restrict recovery under specific indemnities, the tax covenant, completion obligations, price adjustments and title warranties. A specific indemnity is of little value if general exclusions undermine it.

**Push back:**
- Confine the general regime expressly to **general warranty claims**. Set out separate treatment for fundamental warranties, tax, specific indemnities, payment obligations and price adjustments.
- Negotiate a higher general cap, a lower de minimis and basket, and a **tipping basket**—recovery of all qualifying claims once the basket is exceeded—not merely the excess. Aggregate related claims to avoid artificial fragmentation.
- Seek at least 24 months for general warranties, allowing review across two reporting cycles. Check for separate deadlines to commence proceedings and onerous notice requirements.
- Preserve fraud and fraudulent concealment carve-outs and rights that cannot lawfully be excluded. Review exclusive-remedy and non-reliance wording under NSW law rather than assuming it is fully effective.

The 20% cap is not inherently unacceptable, but its adequacy depends on the rest of the protections and Seller creditworthiness.

### 2. Fundamental title and capacity warranties need separate protection

**Seller position:** Same cap and time limits as general warranties, supposedly for administrative simplicity.

**Buyer concern:** Paying AUD 24 million but recovering at most AUD 4.8 million for defective title is unacceptable risk allocation. Administrative simplicity is no justification.

**Push back:**
- Separate fundamental warranties covering capacity, authority, ownership of all issued shares, absence of encumbrances and rights to acquire shares.
- Seek a cap of at least the purchase price and a materially longer claim period, commonly negotiated at six or seven years, with NSW limitation rules and execution form checked.
- Exclude these claims from the general de minimis and basket.

DD-012 is evidence of registered ownership, **not a substitute for verification** of beneficial ownership, encumbrances, capital structure, options or competing rights. Require appropriate searches, corporate records and completion transfer deliverables.

### 3. Blanket disclosure and constructive knowledge could hollow out warranties

**Seller position:** Everything contained or referred to in the data room and public records is disclosed; knowledge includes matters discoverable by the Buyer or its advisers.

**Buyer concern:** This shifts the risk of obscure, incomplete or indirectly referenced information to Wattlebridge. It could defeat claims even where the Buyer did not actually know the relevant facts.

**Push back:**
- Require **fair disclosure with sufficient detail to identify the nature and scope of the matter**, preferably against the relevant warranty.
- Reject unrestricted disclosure by reference and blanket public-register disclosure. If limited general disclosures are accepted, specify their sources and scope.
- Freeze and retain an indexed copy of the disclosure data room.
- Delete the “discoverable” test and imputation of all advisers’ knowledge. Prefer no knowledge exclusion; any compromise should be limited to actual knowledge of named Buyer individuals.
- Ensure disclosure and Buyer knowledge do **not** qualify agreed specific indemnities, completion obligations or price adjustments.

The 22 September disclosure snapshot also needs updating through signing and Completion. New disclosures should not automatically waive claims or force the Buyer to complete.

### 4. Bluefen consent: a material completion condition, not an endeavours obligation

**Facts:** Approximately AUD 3.6 million revenue—30% of FY26 revenue—is associated with Bluefen. Consent clause 11.2 has associated conditions in clause 11.3. No final consent or evidence of satisfaction is supplied.

**Buyer concern:** Delivery of a written consent alone may not satisfy its conditions or preserve the contract on acceptable terms.

**Push back:**
- Make effective consent **and satisfaction of all associated conditions** a Buyer-waivable condition precedent.
- Require consent covering the actual transaction, without adverse pricing changes, termination rights or other unacceptable conditions.
- Obtain the underlying contract, consent and supporting evidence.
- Include a long-stop date and Buyer termination right if the condition is not met.

Reasonable endeavours is an interim obligation, not a replacement for the required outcome.

### 5. Riverlark: repayment and security release must be part of Completion

**Facts:** Approximately AUD 3.2 million remains outstanding. No final discharge is included; the Seller proposes release after Completion.

**Buyer concern:** That exposes Wattlebridge to acquisition debt and continuing security contrary to the debt-free/cash-free baseline, as well as possible change-of-control default.

**Push back:**
- Obtain a binding lender payout statement covering principal, interest, fees and break costs.
- Include repayment in the completion funds flow and secure effective releases through agreed simultaneous completion arrangements.
- Require release of relevant security and guarantees, with controlled registration-removal mechanics.
- Review any required change-of-control waiver or consent pending discharge.
- Deduct the relevant debt in the equity-price calculation or require Seller-funded repayment, **without double counting**.

An unsecured promise to deliver a release afterwards is insufficient.

### 6. Completion bonuses: an omitted economic liability

**Facts:** Conditional bonuses total AUD 420,000 and are absent from the funds flow. On-costs are unresolved.

**Buyer concern:** Calling these “a matter for the Seller” does not prevent Paperbark—and therefore the Buyer—from funding them after Completion.

**Push back:**
- Review entitlement, payment timing and continued-employment conditions.
- Allocate the transaction-triggered liability expressly to the Seller through payment, a price deduction or a funded retention.
- Quantify applicable superannuation, payroll tax and other on-costs.
- Prevent double counting across debt, working capital and transaction expenses.
- Include an indemnity for unpaid Seller-allocated amounts.

Distinguish genuinely Buyer-agreed post-completion retention incentives from pre-existing sale bonuses.

### 7. Ironquay: the problem is ownership, not just an AUD 180,000 invoice

**Facts:** SOW3 title transfers only on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. AUD 180,000 is recorded as open; payment and assignment evidence are missing.

**Buyer concern:** A payment-only indemnity may not cover inability to use or exploit important IP, third-party claims, replacement costs or business disruption. The evidence does **not** conclusively establish non-payment, but ownership remains unverified.

**Push back:**
- Verify all relevant fees and obtain payment evidence and an effective confirmatory assignment or other adequate chain-of-title documentation.
- If the materials are business-critical, require resolution before Completion.
- Broaden the specific indemnity to cover the consequences of defective ownership and relevant third-party claims, with separately negotiated limits and duration.
- Assess IP warranties separately rather than accepting that all IP risk is “settled” under the general regime.

### 8. Export/privacy incident: investigate without overstating the evidence

**Facts:** A download link went to an unintended external address; approximately 1,240 records may be involved. Access, exact scope and notification requirements remain unknown.

**Buyer concern:** The Seller’s assertion that it is not expected to be material is unsupported. Equally, the documents do not establish a confirmed notifiable breach or quantified loss.

**Push back:**
- Require preservation of evidence, access-log review, confirmation of the dataset, containment and a documented investigation.
- Obtain an assessment of applicable privacy, contractual and notification obligations.
- Require appropriate remediation and consultation with the Buyer, without delaying legally required action.
- Seek a specific indemnity for the pre-completion incident, covering investigation, remediation and third-party exposure to the extent legally recoverable.
- Reassess completion conditions or retention once the findings establish severity.

### 9. Sandbar renewals: assess the aggregate commitment and its timing

**Facts:** Three related renewals total AUD 330,000. The materials do not establish whether they are unavoidable, terminable, accrued or ordinary-course.

**Buyer concern:** The Seller’s ordinary-course characterisation is unproven. Splitting related commitments into three AUD 110,000 contracts should not circumvent approval thresholds.

**Push back:**
- Read DD-008 and DD-011 together and establish renewal dates, service periods, termination rights and total commitments.
- Aggregate related commitments under interim operating covenants and require Buyer approval where appropriate.
- Determine accounting and price treatment from the facts.

Do **not** automatically deduct AUD 330,000: genuine future operating costs are not necessarily debt-like liabilities. Conversely, accrued liabilities or Seller-driven exceptional commitments should not escape adjustment merely by being labelled renewals.

### 10. Tax: do not leave historical exposure under an 18-month general regime

**Buyer concern:** Historical tax liabilities may emerge well after general warranty protection expires. Disclosure of a risk should not necessarily transfer its economic burden to the Buyer.

**Push back:**
- Require a separate tax covenant/indemnity for relevant pre-completion tax.
- Negotiate separate caps, exclusions and survival aligned with applicable assessment periods and a claims buffer.
- Address tax-return control, audits, settlements, cooperation and transaction-related tax liabilities.
- Ensure the general basket, disclosure and knowledge exclusions do not inadvertently defeat tax protection.

### 11. Lease and Mossvale: pursue the obligations actually shown

- **Office lease:** The supplied material identifies notification, not landlord consent. Verify and satisfy the notification obligation; do not invent a consent condition.
- **Mossvale:** An assignment restriction does not by itself establish consent is needed for a share sale. Check the full agreement for change-of-control or deemed-assignment wording before requiring consent.

These distinctions keep negotiations focused on evidenced risks.

## Recommended negotiating priorities

1. **Rebuild the claims architecture:** restrict general limitations, narrow disclosure and knowledge exclusions, and protect fundamental, tax and specific-indemnity claims.
2. **Secure completion certainty:** effective Bluefen consent and conditions; Riverlark payout and releases; verified title and transfer deliverables.
3. **Correct the economics:** account for debt, bonuses and on-costs; investigate Sandbar treatment without assuming all future costs are deductible.
4. **Resolve or ring-fence known risks:** Ironquay ownership and the export/privacy incident.
5. **Check recovery security:** assess Harbourglass’s post-sale ability to pay and negotiate retention, escrow or a suitable guarantee where needed.

**Bottom line:** Do not complete on the strength of disclosure and post-completion promises where the Buyer needs consent, clear title, debt discharge or a funded allocation of known liabilities.
